Architecture and security

What runs on your machine, how encryption and certificates work, who can see what, and the limits we haven't closed yet.

Packet flow · Client isolation · Encryption and DNS-01 HTTPS · Threat model · Host isolation and supply chain · Known limits

Packet flow and trust boundaries

Hogman separates the data plane (traffic between members and shares) from the control plane (device keys, ACL policy, and pen DNS). Only the control plane's front door listens on the public internet.

Data plane (member browser to a share — control server sees ciphertext only)

  Browser
    │  PAC sends *.<pen>.pens.hogman.network to 127.0.0.1:<port>;
    │  all other traffic goes directly to the internet as usual
    ▼
  hogman-join  (unprivileged Go binary, userspace tsnet — blind TCP :443 CONNECT tunnel)
    │  1. Queries pen DNS (port 53 inside mesh) -> random CGNAT 100.x / fd7a:: address
    │  2. Verifies resolved IP is an enrolled peer via tsnet WhoIs (never dials LAN/127.0.0.1)
    │  3. Enforces :443 only (D-11)
    ▼
  [ WireGuard E2E encrypted tunnel + inner TLS 1.3 ]   (direct UDP, or DERP relay ciphertext)
    ▼
  hogman-join share  (separate tsnet server node, local CertMagic keypair)
    │  Serves local folder via Go os.Root (symlink escape refused) or reverse-proxies localhost:<port>
    ▼
  Your app or folder

Control plane & certificate issuance (metadata visible; no application payloads)

  *.gate.hogman.network  -->  Shared Caddy front door (strict path allowlist + TLS wildcard)
                                │
                                ▼
                        Per-pen container network (pen-<name>-core, 4 containers)
                          ├── Headscale   (random 100.64.0.0/10 IPs, WireGuard keys, ACL grants)
                          ├── core-mesh   (Tailscale node terminating mesh DNS & portal IP)
                          ├── Registrar   (Go ledger, pen DNS :53, Unix socket API to portal)
                          └── Portal      (home.<zone> Caddy + CertMagic local key)

  ns1.hogman.network     -->  Authoritative miekg/dns server (:53 UDP/TCP)
                                Serves ONLY _acme-challenge.* TXT, SOA, NS, CAA (no A/AAAA under pens.)

The local proxy inside hogman-join is a blind TCP CONNECT tunnel. It forwards encrypted TLS bytes straight between your browser and the share without terminating, inspecting, or re-signing TLS.

What runs on your computer (and what it refuses to touch)

Joining a pen downloads and runs one unprivileged static Go binary (hogman-join) embedding Tailscale's userspace tsnet networking stack.

  • No kernel interface, no daemon as root: hogman-join creates no TUN device, edits no /etc/hosts or system DNS resolvers, never asks for sudo, and leaves any existing Tailscale installation untouched.
  • No OS root CA (D-18): Your computer validates pen certificates with its normal operating system and browser trust store. Nothing is injected into your root store, so a pen cannot mint certificates for any site outside its zone.
  • PAC-scoped loopback proxy: hogman-join binds to 127.0.0.1:<port> and serves a /proxy.pac rule matching only the pen zones you joined. /status and /proxy.pac reject requests whose Host header is not loopback, preventing DNS-rebinding reads from random web pages. Plain http:// requests to pen names receive an immediate local 308 redirect before crossing the mesh.
  • WhoIs-pinned dialing (red-team fix): Left unguarded, tsnet.Dial falls back to the host OS network when given a non-peer IP. Regardless of what the pen's DNS returns, hogman-join only dials addresses inside 100.64.0.0/10 or fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48 that lc.WhoIs confirms belong to an enrolled node in that pen. A hostile pen can never pivot your browser to 127.0.0.1, LAN routers, or another tailnet.
  • Personal devices stay unreachable: Member devices accept zero inbound connections. Putting a site or folder into the pen with hogman-join share spins up a separate server device (tag:server). Folder shares open targets through Go's os.Root (refusing symlinks pointing outside the shared directory). Share nodes use separate single-use invite tokens marked for=share, which personal joins reject.

Transport, encryption, and public HTTPS on private IPs (D-18)

Every request to a share is encrypted twice, with keys held by the two endpoints:

  1. Outer WireGuard tunnel: Direct peer-to-peer WireGuard encrypted end to end between devices. When NAT traversal cannot establish a direct UDP path, traffic flows over the pen's DERP relay as WireGuard ciphertext.
  2. Inner TLS 1.3 with standard web certificates: Each share generates its own keypair and obtains its own certificate directly using embedded CertMagic. TLS private keys never leave the sharer's computer, and traffic stays inside the WireGuard tunnel (so browsers never connect directly without WireGuard).

Obtaining publicly trusted certificates without exposing pen servers to the public internet works via split-horizon DNS-01:

  • No public addresses: ns1.hogman.network (an authoritative server built on miekg/dns) is delegated for pens.hogman.network and _acme-challenge.gate.hogman.network. It serves only SOA, NS, CAA, and short-lived _acme-challenge.* TXT records (10-minute expiry, capped at 2 live records per name). Every other query under pens.hogman.network returns empty NODATA: pen and share names never resolve on the open internet.
  • Strict ownership + weekly caps: When a share requests a certificate, it calls the pen's registrar over the mesh (POST /api/acme/txt). The registrar verifies the caller's mesh identity against live Headscale nodes, enforces serverMayUse (a share can only write challenges for names pointing solely to itself, never home, nodes, or another share's name), and calls challenge-dns with that pen's hashed per-pen API token (capped at 10 distinct new names per pen per week).
  • CAA + CA failover: pens.hogman.network publishes 0 issue "letsencrypt.org; validationmethods=dns-01", 0 issue "pki.goog; validationmethods=dns-01", and 0 issuewild ";". Primary issuance uses Let's Encrypt with ACME Renewal Information (ARI, RFC 9773). If a CA returns rate limits (429), 5xx errors, or transport failures — never on DNS or ownership errors — CertMagic fails over to Google Trust Services using single-use External Account Binding (EAB) credentials minted lazily over the mesh. Persistent retry backoff (up to 1 hour) survives service restarts so failing shares do not hammer CAs.
  • Wildcard front doors: Hosted pens share *.gate.hogman.network (0 issue ";" plus account-pinned issuewild CAA) so pen names stay out of front-door Certificate Transparency entries.

Two public-certificate trade-offs to know before joining:

  • Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962): Every issued certificate — meaning pen names and share hostnames such as photos.yourpen.pens.hogman.network — appears in public CT logs by design. Site contents and traffic are never exposed, only the names.
  • Cookie/same-site scope until PSL listing (D-19): Every hosted pen lives under pens.hogman.network. Until pens.hogman.network is on the Public Suffix List (after launch eligibility), browsers treat pens as sibling subdomains for cookies and same-site requests. Use a separate browser profile if you join a pen you do not fully trust.

Threat model and trust boundaries

Hogman is private, not anonymous. Here is what each party can see or do, and what stops them:

AdversaryWhat they can see or doWhat stops them
Passive ISP, Wi-Fi, or internet scanner Sees UDP WireGuard or HTTPS DERP ciphertext to the relay IP, plus public CT names. Cannot resolve pen A/AAAA records or probe mesh ports. Zero public addresses under pens., strict front-door allowlist on control hosts, end-to-end WireGuard + inner TLS 1.3.
Compromised DERP relay or front-door proxy Sees WireGuard node keys, packet timing/sizes, and front-door HTTP traffic to the control endpoint. Relay never holds WireGuard private keys or share TLS private keys. Control traffic is only coordination and join pages.
Malicious member inside your pen Has a valid mesh identity and can resolve share names in the pen. Headscale ACL grants :443 toward tag:server devices only (D-11: no :22, no member-to-member connections, no exit nodes or subnet routes). Registrar enforces serverMayUse so shares cannot steal names or mint certs for another share. Keepers can suspend or kick in ~2 s; kicked names stay held for 90 days.
Hostile pen targeting your laptop Controls the pen's DNS responses, Headscale map, and invite payload. Unprivileged binary (no root/TUN), no OS root CA, client-side zone validation, loopback Host check, WhoIs dial pin (blocks 127.0.0.1 / LAN / cross-tailnet DNS tricks), and :443-only proxy gate.
Compromised keeper or hosting server (control plane) Sees: member list, enrolled device keys/IPs, online times, and mesh DNS lookups. Could in principle: add a rogue device, rewrite ACLs, or mint a DNS-01 challenge TXT record for a pen name. Cannot passively read direct WireGuard traffic or share TLS private keys. Any rogue certificate forged via DNS-01 control must be logged in public CT logs, making silent MITM detectable. Honest account keys cannot be recovered by support (D-16).

Host isolation and supply chain

  • Hosted control plane (D-24), open source (AGPL): Every pen runs in its own isolated Docker network (pen-<name>-core) with its own SQLite database, Headscale instance, keys, and UDP relay port — pens share no container network with one another. Software versions are pinned in core/compose.yaml.
  • Container & host hardening: Pen containers and the shared Caddy front door run non-root (uid 65532), read-only (tmpfs for /tmp), with cap_drop: [ALL] and no-new-privileges. The front door replaces Headscale catch-all routing with an explicit path allowlist (/ts2021, /key, /derp*, /bootstrap-dns, /machine/ping-response, /health; 404 otherwise) plus HSTS, X-Frame-Options: DENY, CSP, nosniff, and Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1.
  • Registrar & host service isolation: The registrar's mesh/admin HTTP API listens only on a kernel-enforced Unix domain socket shared between registrar and portal (no loopback TCP), matches X-Forwarded-For IPs against live Headscale nodes, and enforces CSRF checks (Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site + Content-Type: application/json). Host services (challenge-dns and gate-cert) run as dedicated unprivileged users under strict systemd sandboxing (ProtectSystem=strict, syscall filters, LoadCredential secrets, UMask=0077). Used public pen names are burned permanently (D-21).
  • No account recovery (D-16): Losing every device means starting a new account with a new invite. There is no password reset or operator backdoor to talk your way past. (Pen owners should appoint a second owner.)
  • Infrastructure as code & verifiable builds: Public DNS changes only via reviewed PRs with dnscontrol preview + locked approval (D-23). Release binaries are built exclusively in GitHub Actions with SLSA build provenance and verified by deploy/release.sh before publishing; anyone can verify a downloaded binary:
$ gh attestation verify hogman-join --repo celtiberi/hogman

Our full self-audit against OWASP ASVS, CIS Docker/Linux, and SLSA (plus every fix shipped) is in docs/security/audit-2026-11.md, and the full PKI architecture note is in docs/security/public-certificates.md.

Known limits and deliberate omissions

  • Not independently audited yet: Reviewed internally against standard checklists, not yet tested by an external security firm.
  • Device keys on disk: A member's pen identity currently lives in user-readable state files rather than hardware/TPM/Keychain binding; copying those files lets someone use that device slot until revoked.
  • Auto-update verification: hogman-join update checks HTTPS transport and published SHA256SUMS rather than a key pinned inside the binary (signed updates planned).
  • Public Suffix List (D-19): pens.hogman.network is not yet listed on the PSL, so use separate browser profiles across mutually untrusted pens.
  • HTTPS to servers only (D-11): No SSH, arbitrary UDP/TCP, member-to-member connections, exit nodes, or LAN subnet routing — omitted by design to minimize client and lateral attack surface.
